Compound events where droughts end with heavy precipitation can lead to damage to infrastructure,
crops and ecosystems that exceed those of an isolated drought or heavy precipitation event due to
increased ﬂooding and runoff from the hardened dry ground. Based on regional climate models we
show that the occurrence of these compound events (drought ending with one in 100-dayprecipitation
event) during summer in Europe increases by around 35% (+/−22%) for both the mid-century and
end-of-century future projections with an intermediate emission scenario compared to present-day.
This increase to 97% (+/−84%) for droughts ending in a more extreme precipitation event (occurring
approximately once a year) and is greater than the increase in drought and heavy precipitation events
separately. Central and Southern Europe are likely to experience the strongest absolute increase.
Results highlight the need to prepare for and adapt to these rare but potentially devastating events.
Climate change has led to an intensiﬁcation of both droughts and extreme
precipitation events1. Periods of droughts can cause soil water repellency
(SWR) which reduces the ability of water to inﬁltrate soils, leading to an
increased chance of ﬂooding and soil erosion if a heavy precipitation event
would occur2,3. If wildﬁres occurred during the drought, it would also
amplify the runoff due to the impermeability of burned soil4. Isolated events
ofdroughtsorextremeprecipitation canhavealargeimpact,butcompound
events where droughts end in a heavy or extreme precipitation event can
cause more damage with larger implications economically5–7. For example
in mid-August 2022, during a period of extreme drought over Europe with
estimated damages to 40 billion EUR8, thunderstorms with heavy pre-
cipitation occurred. The precipitation caused ﬂash ﬂooding and additional
damages estimated to over 247 million EUR over Western and Central
Europe9,10.
The shift between a drought season to a pluvial season have become
more frequent globally in the last 30 years11. Precipitation whiplashes from
dry to wet extremes (and wet to dry extremes) are more frequent for mid-
and high-latitudes and these whiplash events will become more frequent
withglobalwarmingbothglobally,andoverEuropewithsomeuncertainties
over the Mediterranean12,13. Rezvani, Na and Najaﬁ14 found that compound
lagged drought and wet spells will become more frequent and that the
transition time between them will decrease with global warming over
Northwest and North America15. Events where dry periods ends in heavy
precipitation periods have been found to increase with two or three times by
the end of the century over East Asia16. The increase in these types of events
will reduce rice crops and lead to reduced food security17.
Global Climate Models (GCMs) show a large spread in precipitation
for historical and future projections, but the models agree that global
warmingleadstofewerdayswithlightprecipitationandahigherprobability
ofheavyprecipitationdaysandachangeinprecipitationvariability3,18,19.The
increase in extreme precipitation with global warming has been found in
both observations and model data over Europe since the 1950s1,20,21, and
GCMs agree on the sign of the projected increase in heavy precipitation
(>99th percentile) across all latitudes22, and speciﬁcally over land and in the
extratropic23. However, there are uncertainties in the magnitude of heavy
precipitation increase, as well as which regions that will experience an
increase in mean precipitation or a drying1.

In contrast to previous studies where a period of drought is followed by
a pluvial period, we will analyze compound summer events where the
drought periods end in both a heavy (once every 100 days) and extreme
precipitation event (once a year) over Europe (see Methods). We will use
both gridded observations and reanalysis and compare the results for his-
torical periods to different RCMs as well as future projections with two

Results
Historical compound events
Figure 1 shows the relative change between the reference period
(1951–1980) and the two historical periods. Both E-Obs and ERA-5 show
around a 10% decrease (25% decrease for ERA-5 for 1981–2000) in severe
drought summer days where the SPI-3 index is below -1.5 (classiﬁed as
severe drought26), compared to the reference period. Supplementary Fig. S1
also shows that there is an increase in droughts south of 45 degrees north
during spring and summer, while over the entire European domain there is
relatively little change, similar to results in ref. 27 with an increase in
droughts over the Mediterranean and a decrease in Scandinavia and Russia.
For the regional climate models the change in severe drought days differs
more, both between the time periods and models. Biases in RCMs are due to
both the underlying GCM and the regional downscaling model28. The
COSMO ensemble mean downscaled from CESM1-CAM4 shows a high
increaseinsummerdayswithseveredroughtoverthehistoricalperiods,and
nearly all individual ensemble members show this (Supplementary Fig. S3).
Indicating that with a drying GCM, the natural variability shown by the
COSMO members is smaller than the actual natural variability29. The dif-
ference between observations, reanalysis and the RCMs however are com-
parable to the differences between the COSMO members.
For the extreme precipitation events, all datasets show an increase
compared to the reference period, and a larger increase for the 99.7th per-
centile than the lower 99th percentile (15–60%), similar to previous
studies20,30. However, the COSMO ensemble and the NorESM1-M model
downscaled with the HIRHAM5 v3 regional model show a larger increase
between the two percentiles than the other datasets indicating a different
representation of aspects of the hydrological cycle.
The probability of a compound event to occur depends on the prob-
ability of a drought event and of a heavy to extreme precipitation event as
well as the co-occurrence. With a reduction in severe drought days and an
increase in heavy and extreme precipitation days, the observations and
reanalysis results show no large differences between the reference period
compared to the historical periods except for a reduction of the ﬁrst his-
toricalperiodforseveredroughtendinginaheavy(99p) precipitationevent.
Supplementary Fig. S2 shows the decadal occurrence of compound events
over the reference period and the decadal change in occurrence of com-
pound events for the E-Obs dataset, COSMO ensemble mean and COR-
DEX model mean for the historical periods. Compound events as they are
deﬁned in this study, occur all over Europe with around two to four events
per decade, with fewer events on the Iberian Peninsula in observations. For
the later historical period (2001–2020) there are up to four more events
occurring over central Europe compared to the ﬁrst historical period
(1981–2000). Over the reference period, there were several events over
Scandinavia that did not appear in the later historical periods that explains
the negative change.
The RCMs show largely an increase in compound events compared to
the reference period, although with lower change over the model means
compared to observations. The inter model spread in resulting compound
events are largely linked to model differences between the severe drought
days. The change in compound events for the COSMO model shows a
uniform increase over Europe, while the change in CORDEX models shows
both decrease and increasesbetweenthehistoricalperiods. Ifthere is a lower
chance of drought days during a period, there is also a lower chance of
compound events, even though the heavy to extreme precipitation events
increase over time. Similar to the change in severe drought days, there is also
a spread between the results for the RCM downscaled from the same GCM.
The COSMO ensemble mean and DMI-HIRHAM5 downscaled from
NorESM1-M show the highest increases for compound events, especially
for the drought periods ending in extreme precipitation (99.7p) events.

Discussion
Wepresentresultsontheoccurrenceofsummer(May-October)compound
events where drought periods end in a heavy or extreme precipitation event.
As drought periods reduce water inﬁltration into the soil and cause the
ground to become hard and increase the fraction of surface runoff, a heavy
precipitation event during a drought can therefore increase the chance of
ﬂoodingandsoilerosion.Indicesarechosenfroma30-yearreferenceperiod
(1951–1980), based on precipitation to identify severe drought conditions
with SPI less than −1.5 and for heavy and extreme precipitation with events
above two thresholds, 99p and 99.7p, respectively. Results from the two
historical periods show that compound events occur all over Europe in the
E-Obs gridded observational dataset and that this dataset and the ERA-5
reanalysis dataset have comparable results.
We also compare results from RCMs that are downscaled from
global climate models, the COSMO dataset that includes 20 ensemble
members downscaled from the same CESM1-CAM4 climate model
with the strong RCP8.5 forcing scenario and nine CORDEX models
where different regional models downscale four different global cli-
mate models with the intermediate RCP 4.5 and ﬁve with the
stronger RCP 8.5 scenario. Although all models show an increase in
heavy to extreme precipitation over the historical period, there is a
large variation in drought trends over the RCMs. Observations and
reanalysis show a decrease in drought period frequency in the his-
torical periods compared to the reference period, while most RCMs
show an increase in drought periods compared to the reference
period. Trends presented in RCMs are both affected by the trends in
the driving GCM and the RCM parameterizations, the strong drying
in CESM1-CAM4 therefore inﬂuence the COSMO members where
almost all shows an increasing trend in droughts. The differences
between observation, reanalysis and models are found to lie within
the range of natural variability, represented by spread between the
different COSMO members. Since the occurrence of compound
events is dependent on both drought periods and a heavy pre-
cipitation event to occur, the spread in change in drought frequency
results in a model spread for compound events as well. The occur-
rence of compound events in the reference period are comparable
between observations, the COSMO ensemble and the CORDEX
model mean (Supplementary Fig. S2).
The model spread is found for the future projections as well,
where the difference in drought periods is even larger between the

The two GCMs that simulate a strong summer drying over Europe
(CESM1-CAM4 and NorESM1-M) also have RCMs with increases in
drying periods. For the other CORDEX models there is both an
increase, decrease or no large change in the occurrence of summer
drought events. As all models agree on an increase in heavy and
extreme precipitation events, this results in a general increase in
compound ending in a 99p precipitation event with a model mean of
around 35% over Europe, with only one model showing a decrease
for the models using the intermediate RCP 4.5 forcing scenario. This
further strengthens to more than 90% increase when more extreme
precipitation events (99.7p) are considered. The strengthening in the
increase in compound events with strengthening of the precipitation
events show clear similarities to that found for frequency of extreme
precipitation20. The largest increases in the occurrence of future
compound events are found over central and southern Europe. The
results also show that there is a large relative increase in the occur-
rence of future compound events compared to the relative increase in
both drought periods and heavy precipitation events.
As the results in compound events show a strong dependence on
drought periods, future studies should include a drought metric that takes
temperature and evapotranspiration into account, such as the Standard
Precipitation-Evapotranspiration Index (SPEI). Studies on compound
drought and heat events have found an increase globally with an increase in
population being affected33,34 and regionally35,36 with a strong interaction
between precipitation and temperature. Future compound hot-dry events
have also been found to be constrained by the regional precipitation trend37.
Including evapotranspiration in drought calculations would present a
stronger drying trend for historical and future drought events, as well as
extend the region of more frequent compound drought extreme pre-
cipitation events further north as drought areas extend further north with
evapotranspiration included in the calculations24.
Methods
Data
To study the historical evolution of drought and heavy precipitation com-
pound events, observed precipitation from the E-Obs dataset38 version 24 is
used, gridded on a 0.25° × 0.25° degree resolution and available for
1950–2021.Availableobservationsareinterpolatedtothegrid,makingareas
with low station density uncertain39. ERA-5 reanalysis is therefore also
included in the study on the same 0.25° × 0.25° resolution40. As data from
rain gauges are not assimilated in the reanalysis, the precipitation in ERA-5
is independent of observations.
High resolution RCMs better represent the hydrological cycle com-
pared to global models41, and this study uses model results from different
RCMs downscaled from different GCMs. We include 20 members from the
COSMO-CLM model ensemble over Europe29 at ~50 km × 50 km hor-
izontal resolution downscaled from an ensemble of the CESM1-CAM4
simulations42. The COSMO ensemble uses the high emission RCP 8.5 sce-
nario for future projections from 2005 to 2100. Even though there are 20
members of the COSMO model, the results are presented as a model mean,
and this model mean represents one model when calculating total change of
events.
The study also includes nine Euro-CORDEX RCM simulations with
12 km × 12 km resolution, consisting of four different GCMs downscaled
with six different RCMs. All of the CORDEX models are represented on the
same grid, except one (CERFACS-CNRM-CM5: ALADIN63_v2). The
CORDEX data uses the lower emission scenario (RCP 4.5) from 2005 to
2100 because more model results were available for this emission scenario,
in addition to the high emission RCP 8.5 scenario for the (ﬁve) models that
were available.
Euro-CORDEX models tend to overestimate precipitation, however
less in the summer months (JJA) compared to winter months (DJF)28. The
largest overestimation is found over the Iberian Island and Mediterranean.
Biases in the RCMs are due to both the driving GCM and the RCM, and
models using CNRM-CM5 as driver and results with WRF318P tend to
overestimate precipitation over most regions. EC-EARTH also over-
estimates precipitation, although shows good skills over Northern-
Atlantic43, while NorESM1-M and CESM1-CAM4 driving the COSMO
ensemble are drier compared to other CMIP5 models31,32.
Compound metrics
The SPI identiﬁes drought periods with abnormal precipitation deﬁcits
based on time series and can be used to compare drought conditions over

several climatic regions44. Here, the SPI is calibratedfrom the 30-year period
from 1951 to 1980 and is calculated from daily time series to include the
quick shifts with heavy precipitation that can be missed when doing
monthly calculations. SPI-3 monitors meteorological droughts with
reduced soil moisture, but in this study the index is calculated based on the
precipitation accumulated over 90 days before the date of interest using
software based on45. Droughts are deﬁned here as having a SPI lower or
equal to −1.5 standard deviations, which is classiﬁed as severe drought26.
For heavy and extreme precipitation, two thresholds are chosen: events
above the 99th percentile and above the 99.7th percentile, corresponding to
events occurring approximately once every 100 days and once a year,
respectively. Thresholds are calculated based on the reference period
1951–1980 over the whole year. The same precipitation thresholds are used
to identify compound events during drought periods (SPI-3 <= −1.5).
The SPI-3 and precipitation thresholds for all the datasets are
determined from the 30-year reference periods 1951–1980. There are
two historical periods analyzed: 1981–2000 and 2001–2020, and two
future periods used for the RCM data: 2041–2060 (mid-century) and
2081–2100 (end-of-century). Supplementary Fig. S1 shows that the
occurrence of severe drought conditions happens year-round with no
clear high season for the E-Obs data, while summer and compound
events are more frequent during the summer months; May-October
and November south of 45° south. Only the changes in summer
months are evaluated in this study even though the precipitation
thresholds are found from yearly data.
Data availability
The daily gridded precipitation E-OBS datasets are openly available for
download trough the European Climate Assessment&Dataset web site
https://www.ecad.eu/dailydata/. ERA-5 data is openly available through the
CopernicusClimate Data Store (CDS) (https://cds.climate.copernicus.eu/
cdsapp#!/search?type=dataset/). CORDEX data are openly available
through the Earth System Grid Federation (esgf). The COSMO data are
available upon request and people are welcome to contact Erich Fischer
(erich.ﬁscher@env.ethz.ch) to get either processed or raw data.
